newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Political confusion threatens Zaire talks - S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Political confusion threatens Zaire talks - S.Africa.

text.p: Talks in South Africa aimed at making peace in Zaire may be delayed by political confusion in the Central African country, a senior South African diplomat said on Friday.
"Maybe there will be...a later date that will be set aside for the discussions," said Happy Mahlangu, South Africa's deputy high commissioner in London, in an interview with the BBC.
On the eve of the talks, tentatively scheduled for Saturday, rebel leader Laurent Kabila flatly rejected a surprise power-sharing offer from new Zairean Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi.
In Kinshasa, critics said Tshisekedi's offer was not even constitutional.
Mahlangu said this and other political developments threatened to unravel the process.
"On our (South Africa's) side, what we needed to do was facilitate the discussions and of course there won't be any discussions if the two parties are not there," he said.

The Zaire government's negotiating team was in South Africa, meeting officials on Friday to discuss arrangements for the talks, but there was no confirmation that representatives of the rebels had arrived.

A plane carrying senior members of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, led by foreign affairs commissioner Bizima Karaha, left Goma in eastern Zaire on Thursday and had been expected in South Africa later the same day.

However, there was no word, official or otherwise, to indicate the team had indeed arrived. Foreign Ministry officials in Pretoria declined all comment, whether on Mahlangu's statement or on the whereabouts of Kabila's negotiating team.
A Zaire embassy spokesman said details of the talks including their still secret location might be announced on Saturday, but diplomatic sources expressed some doubt.
They said Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's appointment of Tshisekedi -- an opposition leader -- as prime minister had complicated the situation.
The new prime minister has played down the importance of the proposed negotiations in South Africa, saying Kabila was his brother and they did not need to talk through foreign intermediaries.
